articles.title: I am excited to be nervous about Ohio State games this season
articles.summary: As Ohio State fans, we are used to seeing the Buckeyes win games handily. But wins mean so much more when they come with a little bit of adversity. I’m excit...
articles.body:
As Buckeye fans, we live a pretty charmed sporting existence. Ohio State has not lost more than two games in a season — including the postseason — in 15 years, and that was the Luke Fickell season, which barely counts. The Buckeyes have won 85% of their games this century, including three national titles and 11 Big Ten championships. Ohio State is college football's most stable, recession-proof program.

This year, I am looking forward to something that has been in relatively short supply during much of the Buckeyes' 21st-century dominance. I want to be nervous.

I want to spend a Saturday afternoon with the vague, nagging sensation that I could throw up at any moment. I want to be so invested in what I am watching on screen that I forget to breathe for an uncomfortably — and dangerously — long time. I want to go into a game and have something more to worry about than whether my favorite team is going to win by 40 or 50 points.

Back in May, I wrote about why I was legitimately excited by the possibility that Ohio State could lose three or even four games this season. Now, of course, I don't actually want them to lose any game, but the possibility that they could makes the prospect of tuning in each week, especially for the season's half-dozen or so marquee matchups, that much more exciting.

The Buckeyes go on the road to play Texas, Iowa, Indiana, and USC and host Illinois, Oregon, and Michigan. Six of those teams are ranked in the preseason poll (Illinois is receiving votes), and three are in the top six. When you factor in games against competent Nebraska and Northwestern teams, there are legitimate opportunities for stress sprinkled throughout basically the entire season.

That doesn't mean that all of those games will come down to the final possession. Some might even end up being blowouts in Ohio State's favor. But every year, television talking heads and internet prognosticators spend entire weeks convincing us that the Buckeyes' trip to play some random 6-3 Big Ten team is the superest, sneakiest upset pick in recent memory, only for Ohio State to be up 31-6 midway through the third quarter.

But this year, there are enough legitimately excellent opponents, hostile environments, awkward scheduling spots, and teams with comparable talent that it seems almost impossible for Ohio State to sleepwalk through the regular season. Regardless of what their eventual record is, I think that's a good thing.

Obviously, winning is fun. I am not going to sit here and pretend that I have somehow spiritually transcended caring about the scoreboard. If Ohio State beats every team by 40 points on the way to another national championship, I promise that I will find a way to weather such a terrible burden. But there is more to being a fan — and being a human — than just the momentary dose of dopamine that comes from accomplishing something that was never really in doubt to begin with.

Sports aren't compelling if every game is a foregone conclusion. We love sports, and college football in particular, because they open us up to a much wider range of emotions than we normally experience in our day-to-day lives: anticipation, frustration, relief, anger, surprise, fear, joy — sometimes all within the span of three hours and usually because a 20-year-old we have never met caught or dropped a pass.

The strange downside of Ohio State's overwhelming consistency is that winning can stop feeling like an accomplishment and start feeling like the status quo. Beat an overmatched opponent by 35? Fine. That's what you were supposed to do. Win by 17? Why couldn't the offensive line block anybody? Why did the secondary give up that touchdown? Is everything collapsing?

At some point, we can optimize the joy right out of fandom, and where's the fun in that? To me, victories simply mean more when losing feels possible.

Think about the Ohio State wins that live deepest in your memory. Chances are they weren't 56-7 wins in which the Buckeyes had their third-string quarterback handing the ball off by the middle of the third quarter. They were games where something went wrong; games where your stomach hurt; games where Ohio State had to survive something. They were Holy Buckeye; they were 85 yards through the heart of the south; they were Scoop and Sawyer.

The struggle is what gives the victory texture, what gives it meaning. Wins are simply more satisfying when they follow uncertainty and adversity. To me, that is what fandom is all about. The possibility of heartbreak is part of what makes our bond with the team stronger and their accomplishments sweeter.

And as we saw last season, if teams don't face adversity in the regular season, when they finally do find themselves in harrowing situations, they might not have the scars and calluses to finish the job. Ohio State will be better prepared for December and January this year if it spends September, October, and November playing games in which mistakes actually have consequences and winning isn't a foregone conclusion. There will be moments when the Buckeyes have to respond to a turnover, a blown coverage, an opposing crowd losing its mind, or — heaven forbid — actually trailing in the second half. And frankly, I think going through some of that adversity is good for us fans, too.

That is part of what makes fandom so ridiculous, and so meaningful. Regardless of how inspirational (or infuriating) my little blog posts might be, I have absolutely no impact on whether Ohio State wins or loses. Yet I can still tear up when the Buckeyes raise a trophy, and occasionally when they don't.

That is the deal we make when we care about something we can't control. Giving your heart to anything — a person, a career, a cause, a passion, a football team — means accepting the possibility that it might get broken. Take away that risk entirely, and you also take away some of what makes the reward mean something.

So no, I never want Ohio State to lose. I don't want them to have three losses, or two, or even one. I want the Buckeyes to go 16-0. I just want to spend a few Saturdays genuinely wondering whether they will.

I want opponents to land punches and for Ohio State to have to punch back. I want fourth quarters where the outcome is still undecided. I want to pace around my living room, complain about officiating, question every play call, and spend three hours allowing the decision-making of people born after I graduated from OSU to dictate my emotional well-being.

Because when the clock finally hits zero after one of those games, winning feels different. It isn't simply the expected result arriving on schedule; it's relief, exhilaration, exhaustion, and joy all boiling over at once.

That is what I am looking forward to this season. Not just seeing whether Ohio State can win every Saturday, but feeling like, for once, they might not.

articles.title: “Stayed down": Prophet Brown remains humble after securing first career interception in USC's 39-0 blowout
articles.summary: Fresno State quarterback Jayden Mandal threw a lob pass that sixth-year senior safety Prophet Brown intercepted...
articles.body:
The USC Trojans completely shut out (39-0) the Fresno State Bulldogs, marking their second consecutive win of the season, on Friday. Under new defensive coordinator Gary Patterson, the team put on an outstanding performance, building on last week's 42-26 victory against San Jose State as a big step forward.

The Trojans' defense held Fresno State to 116 yards for the entire game, allowing 49 yards up through the third quarter. During this stellar effort, the defense recorded two safeties and forced two turnovers.

The Bulldogs tried to stop Trojans' running game at the start, but they managed to enter USC territory only once all game. In the first quarter, Fresno State quarterback Jayden Mandal threw a lob pass that sixth-year senior safety Prophet Brown intercepted, marking the first interception of his career.

Brown, who is part of the 2021 recruiting class, was the presumptive starter at the nickel position last year, but he broke his hip during fall camp. Playing his third college defensive season in three years, Brown called this moment 'everything' for him.

"It meant everything, Brown said. "I didn't do a lot of stuff behind the scenes, you know, just worked, worked, stayed down, and for the the opportunity to come, you know, thank God for it."

On the offensive side, Trent Mosley made two touchdown catches. On defense, Kennedy Urlacher forced a fumble from Mandal, while Alex Graham delivered a crucial sack in the third quarter, earning the game's second safety. This late stand preserved the Trojans' first shutout since September 2024 (against Utah State, 48-0).

Head coach Lincoln Riley praised Urlacher's performance (three tackles, two sacks), saying

"He's starting to settle in more and more to a system and understand it, and once he goes and turns it loose, you feel his speed and his physicality on the field."

Indeed, Riley made it clear after the game that the team still has quite a few things to clean up. He said the team had two fumbles, couldn't convert third- and fourth-and-one in the red zone, and he himself also made some bad calls.

"We had a couple of couple things that we didn't like... where we messed up a few things," Riley said. "I had a couple bad calls. And then obviously the turnovers."

USC (2-0) will now host Louisiana-Lafayette Ragin' Cajuns at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in their next non-conference game next Saturday, Sept. 12. This game will be broadcast live at 8 p.m. PDT on the Big Ten Network.

articles.title: Liverpool have a new £100m attacker, and it isn't Bradley Barcola
articles.summary: Bradley Barcola was Liverpool's biggest signing of the window. The Frenchman cost the club around the same as what they spent on Alexander Isak and, while he...
articles.body:
Bradley Barcola was Liverpool's biggest signing of the window.

The Frenchman cost the club around the same as what they spent on Alexander Isak and, while he's only played a few minutes for the Reds, he already looks like he's going to fit right in.

After Yan Diomande's deal fell through, Barcola was their main target and, even though it took until almost deadline day to confirm the move, he's likely to be worth every minute of the wait.

He can play anywhere across the front three if needed and, since he's only 24 years old, there's plenty of time for him to grow.

However, as good as Barcola is, he's not actually the next £100 million attacker that Liverpool have among their ranks.

Cody Gakpo has been reborn by Andoni Iraola at Liverpool

Last season, fans wanted to do everything in their power to get rid of Cody Gakpo .

The 2025-26 season was arguably the worst of his career in a Liverpool shirt.

The Dutchman only bagged nine goals across all competitions and only managed to muster up six assists for his teammates.

Slot even played him in his preferred positions of left-wing and striker but he still just didn't meet expectations.

So, when Manchester City and Tottenham's £85 million bids came in at the end of the window, everyone wanted Liverpool to accept.

But, after his performance against Ipswich on Friday night, every Liverpool fan you ask would be happy that the move wasn't sanctioned.

Gakpo managed to create two goals for Isak and was easily Iraola's best player at Portman Road.

Indeed, he was used in his preferred position of left-wing but, for one reason or another, the 27-year-old just seems to thrive under the Spaniard's watch which is why he has now become the Reds' next £100 million winger.

Liverpool must figure out the best way to fit all their attackers into their starting XI

At the moment, Isak, Florian Wirtz , Barcola and Gakpo are all fit and ready to play.

Obviously, with Hugo Ekitike out of action until who knows when, the Sweden international is going to be the Reds' main number nine.

However, since Gakpo and Barcola both prefer to play on the left, one of them is going to have to make the sacrifice of playing on the right.

For Wirtz, things are okay as, for now, Dominik Szoboszlai is needed in other areas of the pitch so his role as the Reds' main number 10 is also safe for now.

If Iraola can manage to keep all four of them fit throughout the season, they could easily be onto a Premier League-winning season.

Obviously, it's still very early into the campaign so nothing can be guaranteed but, individually, Liverpool easily have some of the world's best players.

So, while Gakpo becoming the Reds' next £100 million winger may have come as a bit of a shock, it's now clear how important the Dutchman actually is to the way that Liverpool play.

Here's hoping he can keep it up and Liverpool out-do themselves.

articles.body:
Serie A side Milan didn't quite see the best of Christian Pulisic in the second half of last season. The player also proved to be disappointing at the World Cup but attempts are underway to tie him down to a new contract.

Daniele Longo reports that a key meeting between Milan owner Gerry Cardinale and Pulisic's entourage – which includes his father, has been scheduled for the middle of next week. They will discuss his situation at the Rossoneri and exercise the option to renew his contract at the club until 2028, as they don't lose him for free next year.

On top of that, parties will also talk about the possibility of Pulisic signing a long-term renewal.

Milan can offer a new deal that will run out in 2031, but the terms of it aren't quite clear yet.

It is likely the matter will be delved into deeper and the finances will be discussed prominently during the meeting.

articles.title: How Tennessee football will honor Wes Rucker in Neyland Stadium press box
articles.summary: Tennessee football will honor the late Wes Rucker in the Neyland Stadium press box with his family and sports reporters before the Furman game.
articles.body:
Tennessee football will honor the late Wes Rucker in the Neyland Stadium press box with his family, fellow sports reporters and UT media relations staff before kickoff of the 2026 season opener.

Rucker, 43, died in a car crash in Knoxville on Feb. 19. The 18th-ranked Vols will play Furman (1-0) on Sept. 5 (3:30 p.m. ET, ESPN+/SEC Network+).

It will be Tennessee's first football game since Rucker's death. And the Tom Elam Press Box unfortunately will be a little quieter without Rucker, the wise-cracking, award-winning sports writer who covered University of Tennessee athletics starting in 2000.

Shortly before kickoff of the Furman game, UT will hold a private dedication for Rucker in the press box. His wife Lauren, son Hank and daughter Rose will be in attendance. They'll be surrounded by Rucker's friends who cover the Vols.

"This will be my first game ever in Neyland without Wes being there watching from this seat," Lauren Rucker posted on X on Sept. 5. "But I know he's watching over us from an even higher vantage point this season and sending us hot takes in the wind. Love you forever, Wes."

Tennessee placed Rucker's photo at his empty seat in the press box with a message familiar to him on X.

"As we begin our 130th season, we remember the late Wes Rucker and welcome you to 'General Neyland's Big Ol' Damn House of Football,' " UT football posted, referencing how Rucker often referred to his gameday workplace at Neyland Stadium.

Rucker covered Tennessee athletics for multiple media outlets. He was a senior writer for 247Sports and most recently served as a writer and host for WBIR in Knoxville. He was a graduate of Knoxville Catholic High and University of Tennessee.

After Rucker's death, Tennessee fans and sports reporters around the country flooded his family with love and support. A GoFundMe established by the family raised $783,000 for Lauren, Hank and Rose. T-shirts were sold to raise additional money. And sports reporters who worked with Rucker throughout the years made additional private donations to honor him.

articles.title: Italian Grand Prix: Who takes pole position?
articles.summary: Follow along as F1 sets the grid for the Italian Grand Prix
articles.body:
Who will take pole position Saturday at the Temple of Speed?

If Friday's two practice sessions were any indication, several drivers will be in the mix ahead of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix. Charles Leclerc topped the timing sheets in FP1, ahead of his Ferrari teammate Lewis Hamilton, while George Russell led the way in the second hour of practice ahead. Russell edged out Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli, the current Drivers' Championship leader.

But with Antonelli facing a ten-place grid penalty for a new power unit, he might be relegated to playing the team game on Saturday to give Russell a tow to pole.

We'll be tracking qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix live on Saturday morning, so check back early and often. And please head to the F1 Community on the brand-new SB Nation app, as we will be chatting in a game thread on the app all morning!

Qualifying gets underway at 10:00 a.m. Eastern.

Update: PIERRE GASLY HAS TAKEN POLE POSITION AT MONZA.

Here is the provisional starting grid for the Italian Grand Prix, which will be filled in during the qualifying session:

Here is how the qualifying hour unfolded. All updates are in Eastern time.

11:04: PIERRE GASLY HAS TAKEN POLE POSITION FOR THE ITALIAN GRAND PRIX.

11:01: Norris, Verstappen, and Russell have all struggled in the first sector so the door is open for … PIERRE GASLY.

10:55: Antonelli completes a lap and he gets to P6, ahead of Norris.

10:52: Initial laps are in. Russell ahead of Piastri, followed by Gasly, Leclerc, Verstappen, Norris, Lindblad, Hamilton, Colapinto, and Antonelli, who did not set a time.

10:48: Antonelli heads out early, with Russell behind. McLaren follows as well. 13 minutes to set the top ten.

10:43: Antonelli, Piastri, Norris, Gasly, Russell, Verstappen, Lindblad, Colapinto, Leclerc, and Hamilton are the ten drivers moving on to Q3. Antonelli already has a grid drop due to a power unit change, and Piastri likely looking at one as well for impeding Lawson at the end of Q2.

10:42: Bortoleto, Bearman, Hulkenberg, Lawson, Sainz, and Ocon are the six drivers eliminated. Leclerc and Hamilton advance … barely, with Leclerc in P9 and Hamilton in P10.

Lawson is out, so Verstappen will be on his own in Q3.

10:39: Piastri might be looking at a penalty here, as he holds up Lawson at the first chicane.

10:38: Under three minutes to go and Hamilton, Bearman, Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, and Ocon are the six drivers in the drop zone

10:34: Norris jumps to P1, but then Piastri takes that spot. Gasly still up in P3 right now, ahead of both Russell and Antonelli.

10:30: "The car is broken on the rear axle again. It's really undriveable in turns 2, 4, 5" says Verstappen on the radio.

10:29: Sainz takes advantage of a tow from Verstappen (who is getting a tow from Lawson) and Sainz goes purple in the first sector.

10:28: Lawson, Verstappen, and Sainz are the three drivers on the track right now. Everyone else still in the pits

10:26: Q2 is underway, with 15 minutes on the clock.

10:24: Gasly, Verstappen, Norris, Colapinto, Lindblad, Antonelli, Russell, Hamilton, Leclerc, Bearman, Piastri, Bortoleto, Lawson, Hulkenberg, Ocon, and Sainz are the 16 drivers into Q2, in that order.

10:1 9: Tsunoda, Albon, Bottas, Perez, Alonso, and Stroll are the six drivers eliminated.

10:17: Alonso out of the car and he's down in P20, so his session is likely over.

10:16: Lawson goes purple in the third sector on a set of softs. His time is only good for P10, but that's a banger of a final sector.

10:14: Five minutes to go in Q1. Hulkenberg, Albon, Bottas, Alonso, Stroll, and Perez the six in the drop zone. Gasly remains in P1 ahead of Verstappen, Colapinto, Antonelli, and Russell rounding out the top five.

10:13: Bearman rockets up to P8, and the young Haas driver should be through. Ocon gets to P16, but he might be in trouble.

10:12: Turning to the battle at the back, Albon, Ocon, Alonso, Bottas, Perez, and Stroll are the six drivers in the drop zone. Hülkenberg on the bubble in P16.

10:11: Oh hello Alpine. Gasly goes P1 and Colapinto P3, sandwiching Verstappen in P2.

Flavio Briatore might be happier today than he was yesterday …

10:11: Initial times from the Merc duo: Antonelli into P2, Russell into P3.

10:09: Lawson slides into P7 on a set of mediums, which is interesting to note. Everyone else on the softs right now.

10:07: Norris picks up a slipstream from an Audi into Turn 11, and completes a lap to slot into P5.

10:06: Verstappen into P1 with a 1:22.631, Hamilton and Piastri slot into P2 and P3 behind him.

Norris has a moment at Turn 1 and will have to go again, as he drives through the chicane.

10:05: According to Alex Jacques, Norris is reporting that the brakes "aren't right" in his MCL40.

10:03: Lawson will be the first to set a time, and he's on a set of mediums while everyone else is on a set of softs. He's facing a grid drop so keep that in mind, as Red Bull has made a chance to his power unit.

10:02: Green light in Monza and we're underway, with Lawson the first driver to take to the track. But we've got Ferraris and McLarens on the circuit as well. No wasting time here.

9:58: Approaching the top of the hour, F1 Opening Titles are on my TV, and now I hear Alex Jacques. Gonna be a fun hour.

9:45: A lot of the early chatter on the F1 channel is focused on what teams are going to use a tow in qualifying. Will Antonelli give Russell a tow, since Antonelli is taking a penalty? Will Williams do that with Albon, who is also taking a penalty, to help Sainz at the end of Q1?

George Russell was fastest again in FP3, ahead of Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen.

Kimi Antonelli finished FP3 in fourth, while Lando Norris rounded out the top five.

articles.title: LeBron James announces partnership with Polymarket
articles.summary: Over the past several months, the sports world has been gradually embracing prediction markets, with Major League Baseball announcing a multi-year partnershi...
articles.body:
Over the past several months, the sports world has been gradually embracing prediction markets, with Major League Baseball announcing a multi-year partnership with Polymarket back in March and the NHL doing so with both Kalshi and Polymarket last year. Now, one of the most high-profile individual athletes on the planet is joining that push.

On Saturday morning, NBA megastar LeBron James, who just signed with the Philadelphia 76ers as a free agent, shared a video on social media seemingly announcing a partnership with Polymarket while announcing something called "Polymarket HQ."

In the rather cryptic video, James can be seen in an elevator looking at a series of buttons that include things like politics, crypto, sports, economy, culture, weather, esports, and technology. James then pushes the button for "sports," and the video cuts to him stepping out of the elevator while "The Largest" by BigXthaPlug plays in the background.

"Welcome to Polymarket HQ. Coming soon," James wrote in the caption , adding an eyes emoji. "In partnership with Polymarket."

Polymarket quickly replied to the post, writing, "Thanks for swinging by our HQ," adding the goat emoji to reference James.

It's not clear what exactly "Polymarket HQ" is – whether it's a physical space, a new feature, or just some sort of advertising campaign – but it is quite clear that LeBron James is now a partner with the prediction market, which is a first for both the NBA and Polymarket.

While the NBA is reportedly in talks with Polymarket , James is the first individual player to sign a partnership with the prediction market and the first individual player that Polymarket has ever signed to such a partnership.

Back in January, golf superstar Bryson DeChambeau signed an ambassador deal with Kalshi in January 2026, making him the first major athlete to partner with a prediction market platform, as he now incorporates Kalshi's markets into his massive YouTube channel. The NFL and PGA Tour, however, reportedly do not allow players to endorse prediction markets.

Formula 1 heads to the iconic Monza circuit this weekend for the Italian Grand Prix and round 13 of the 2026 season.

Kimi Antonelli , who is expected to take a grid penalty at his home race, leads the world championship standings by 59 points to Mercedes teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton , with the Italian having finished second at the last race in Zandvoort.

At the Dutch GP, reigning F1 world champion Lando Norris won his second straight grand prix with a composed drive at Zandvoort, after recording a sublime pole position. Norris is now fourth in the drivers' standings, 83 points behind Antonelli.

Ferrari will be hoping to land a victory at their traditional home race, with Charles Leclerc a two-time winner in Monza and Red Bull's Max Verstappen , who crashed out on the first lap last time out, will be looking to bounce back.
